lessons.title: Why we count teeth
lessons.html:
Why we count teeth

At the abattoir we look at the teeth of cattle, sheep and goats to know how old the animal is. Age is important. Young animals give soft meat. Old animals give tougher meat. In South Africa the age group of a carcass is part of the classification mark, so buyers know what they are paying for.

Milk teeth and permanent teeth

  • A young animal has milk teeth. They are small, narrow and white.
  • As the animal grows, the milk teeth fall out and permanent teeth grow in their place.
  • Permanent teeth are big, broad and look like spades.

Where to look

Cattle, sheep and goats have no front teeth on the top jaw. On top they have a hard pad of gum, called the dental pad. We only count the front teeth (incisors) on the bottom jaw. An adult animal has 8 incisors there.

The permanent incisors come in pairs, from the middle outwards. First the middle 2, then the next 2 on each side, and so on, until there are 8.

Example

Sipho opens the mouth of a steer on the line. He sees 2 big broad teeth in the middle and 6 small milk teeth on the sides. He counts 2 permanent incisors.

Counting is a simple job, but it must be done correctly every time. A wrong count puts the carcass in the wrong age group, and the farmer or the buyer loses money. If you are not sure, ask your supervisor or the classifier to check.

Always count in good light. Use a torch if the area is dark.

lessons.title: Counting teeth safely and recording the result
lessons.html:
Counting teeth safely and recording the result

Work safely

  • Wear your protective clothing: overall or apron, boots, and gloves if your abattoir requires them.
  • On a live animal, only open the mouth when the head is held still in the crush or head clamp. Never put your fingers between the back teeth. The back teeth (molars) can crush a finger.
  • On a head on the line, watch out for knives and hooks around you.
  • Wash your hands and tools after each job, so that you do not spread dirt or germs.

Steps to count

  1. Hold the head steady.
  2. Pull the lower lip down with your thumb.
  3. Look at the bottom front teeth.
  4. Count only the big, broad permanent teeth.
  5. Do not count the small milk teeth.
  6. Say the number out loud and record it.

Age groups used in South Africa

ClassPermanent incisors
A0 (only milk teeth)
AB1 to 2
B3 to 6
Cmore than 6

So the steer with 2 permanent teeth is in age group AB.

Problems you may find

  • A broken or missing tooth: look at the gap and the other teeth. Tell your supervisor.
  • A tooth just coming through the gum: follow your abattoir rule on whether to count it. Ask if you do not know.
  • A dirty mouth: rinse it so you can see clearly.

Write the number on the right sheet or enter it next to the right carcass number. The record must match the carcass. Never guess.

Key points

  • Count only the bottom front teeth.
  • Count only the big permanent teeth, not milk teeth.
  • A = 0, AB = 1 to 2, B = 3 to 6, C = more than 6 permanent teeth.
  • Keep fingers away from the back teeth.
  • Record the count against the correct carcass number.
